title: The Simulation Argument
body: In 2003 the philosopher Nick Bostrom published a trilemma, not a claim: at least one of three things is true — almost no civilization reaches the stage where it could run realistic ancestor-simulations; those that could, choose not to; or we are almost certainly living in one. Bostrom never says which. The novel's own epistemologist, Ajarn Direk, refuses to say the word "simulation" at all — "a cage you can name is furniture." Bostrom's actual argument is colder and more careful than the pop-culture version: it is a statement about probability distributions, not a proof about your Tuesday.
source: Nick Bostrom, "Are You Living in a Computer Simulation?", Philosophical Quarterly 53 (2003)

anchor: Descartes, in a heated room in winter, alone on purpose
title: The Evil Demon
body: The scene is real and specific: Descartes wrote the Meditations in the winter of 1639–40, in a rented room, working the doubt down to its floor. His demon of "the utmost power and cunning" is the direct ancestor of every simulation hypothesis that followed — Putnam's brain in a vat, the Wachowskis' Matrix, Bostrom's ancestor-simulation — all of them re-staging the same 380-year-old move: assume the worst possible deceiver, then ask what, if anything, survives the assumption.
source: René Descartes, Meditations on First Philosophy, Meditation I (1641)

anchor: Zhuangzi dreamed he was a butterfly
title: The Butterfly Dream
body: The narrator is right about the dropped line. The full passage, from the Inner Chapters (Chapter 2, "On the Equality of Things"), ends: "Between Zhuang Zhou and the butterfly there must be some distinction. This is called the transformation of things." The Chinese for that last phrase, wu hua (物化), gives no verdict on which one is real — only that a border exists and gets crossed. Written roughly 2,300 years before Descartes' demon, it arrives at a stranger, less anxious place.
source: Zhuangzi, Inner Chapters, c. 4th century BCE — trans. James Legge, 1891

title: Move 37
body: This happened exactly as told. AlphaGo vs. Lee Sedol, Game 2, 10 March 2016, Seoul. Move 37 was a shoulder hit on the fifth line — a placement so far outside four thousand years of recorded human play that commentators initially assumed a misclick. Professional player Fan Hui's real-time reaction, widely reported, was close to what this chapter gives Direk: "It's not a human move. I've never seen a human play this move." Lee Sedol left the room for fifteen minutes. He retired from professional Go in 2019, citing an opponent that "cannot be defeated."
source: AlphaGo vs. Lee Sedol, Game 2, DeepMind / Google, 10 March 2016

title: The Parable of the Arrow
body: A real sutta, and Golf tells it accurately: the Cula-Malunkyovada Sutta, in which the monk Malunkyaputta refuses to practice until the Buddha answers ten metaphysical questions — is the world eternal, is it not, and so on. The Buddha's answer is not mysticism. It is a refusal of an unanswerable-as-posed question, on the grounds that the man is dying of the wound, not of the unanswered metaphysics.

anchor: The Buddha, whom Golf will not quote directly
title: Foam on the River
body: The five similes are real and precisely rendered: form as foam, feeling as a bubble, perception as a mirage, mental formations as a plantain trunk with no heartwood, consciousness as a magician's trick. None of the five is called false — the text's actual claim, which this chapter states correctly, is that none of them will bear the weight of a house. Māyā, in its oldest technical use, is a statement about load, not about existence.

title: The One Word in the Whole Book
body: By the bible this novel was built from, "simulation" is spoken exactly once, here, by a voice reading from a script. Every other character — Direk especially — declines the word entirely. The scene it lands in, a calm bureaucratic offer of an exit ("Would you like the number?"), is the same beat The Matrix (1999) made globally legible as a choice of pills — minus the myth, minus the color-coding, just paperwork. The film's own production hid a copy of Jean Baudrillard's Simulacra and Simulation, hollowed out as a stash box, in Neo's apartment — a detail confirmed by the Wachowskis themselves, not a reading of the dialogue.
source: The Matrix, dir. Lana & Lilly Wachowski, Warner Bros., 1999 — production detail

anchor: That one," he said, "was not in the game records.
title: Move 37, Returned
body: Direk's homework, three hundred pages earlier, was to bring him one event with no author. What the game commentary actually settled on, in the years after 2016, was not that machines had become unbeatable — that was already known — but that the one remaining argument for human play was creativity of exactly this kind: a move small, free, and chosen, rather than large and calculated. This chapter's closing gesture is built to that specification on purpose.
